extracted.intended_audience: mathematical-olympiad students and problem-solvers (advanced high-school / early undergrad)
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of methods, theorems, and solution-techniques for Olympiad-level problems in number theory, combinatorics, and Euclidean geometry (notably Pell-equation theory, Lucas's theorem, invariant methods, and rotation/Pompeiu techniques).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pell-equation minimal-solution via continued fractions
rubrics_metrics.description: To find all positive integer solutions to u^2 − D v^2 = 1 one first determines a minimal solution (i.e., the solution (u,v) for which u + v√D is minimal and (u,v) ≠ (1,0)). There is a general method using the continued fraction expansion of √D: √D = a1 + 1/(a2 + 1/(a3 + ...)), the sequence a1,a2,a3,... is periodic starting with the second term; let a2,...,am be a cycle of minimal period and let pm/qm be the convergent at the m-th truncation. Then (u1,v1) = (pm,qm) is the minimal solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the continued-fraction period to find (pm,qm). The book sketches this classical algorithm and emphasizes that in many contest problems the minimal solution is easy to guess; once found, further solutions are generated recursively (see recurrence/matrix criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generate Pell solutions by recurrence and matrix form
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the minimal solution (u1,v1) of u^2 − D v^2 = 1, all other solutions (un,vn) are obtained by the recurrence un+1 = u1 un + D v1 vn, vn+1 = v1 un + u1 vn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently use matrix exponentiation: [un; vn] = [[u1, D v1]; [v1, u1]]^n [1; 0]. The text explains multiplication by the conjugate shows the recurrence preserves the Pell identity. Start from the trivial solution (1,0). This is the standard procedure to generate the infinite family of solutions once the minimal one is known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solve generalized Pell ax^2 − b y^2 = 1 via Pell resolvent
rubrics_metrics.description: To solve ax^2 − b y^2 = 1 associate the Pell resolvent u^2 − ab v^2 = 1. If the equation has solutions and (x1,y1) is the smallest positive solution, then all solutions (xn,yn) are given by xn = x1 un + b y1 vn, yn = y1 un + a x1 vn for n ≥ 1, where (un,vn) is the general solution to the resolvent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One may also express this family in matrix form as shown in the text. The resolvent reduces the problem to a standard Pell equation in many cases and allows generating infinite families once the minimal pair for the resolvent and the minimal (x1,y1) are known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative Pell equation solvability and generation
rubrics_metrics.description: The negative Pell equation x^2 − D y^2 = −1 is solvable only for certain values of D. When it is solvable, let (x1,y1) be the minimal solution; then the general solution (xn,yn) (n ≥ 1) is given by xn = x1 un + D y1 vn, yn = y1 un + x1 vn, where (un,vn) is the general solution to the resolvent u^2 − D v^2 = 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the same recurrence/matrix-form techniques as for the +1 Pell equation. The text warns that solvability is not automatic and depends on D; when a minimal solution exists, the resolvent sequence generates all solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special Pell equations x^2 − D y^2 = ±4: reduction and generation
rubrics_metrics.description: Equations x^2 − D y^2 = ±4 are treated separately. If D divisible by 4 incorporate a power of 2 in y to reduce. If D ≡ 2,3 (mod 4) then any solution (x,y) has x,y even and dividing by 4 reduces to X^2 − D Y^2 = ±1. If D ≡ 1 (mod 4) the ±4 cases are nontrivial: when (x1,y1) is the minimal positive solution to x^2 − D y^2 = 4 then all solutions are generated by explicit formulae (including xn+1 = (1/2)(y1 xn + D x1 yn), yn+1 = (1/2)(x1 xn + y1 yn), with (x0,y0) = (2,0)); analogous formulae are given for the −4 case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce by factors of 2 when possible; when D ≡ 1 (mod 4) use the provided half-factor recurrence and powering formulas to generate solutions from the minimal ±4 solution. The text gives both power-form and recurrence-form descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Pell equation x^2 − D y^2 = N: finite-trial reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: The general Pell equation x^2 − D y^2 = N (N ≠ 1) is more complicated. When solvable, finding all solution classes is reduced to an algorithm consisting of a finite number of trials using inequalities involving integers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No simple closed-form generation in general; the standard approach is to reduce to a finite search using bounds/inequalities and congruence constraints, often combined with the structure of the resolvent solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lucas's theorem for binomial coefficients modulo a prime
rubrics_metrics.description: Let p be prime and write n = n0 + n1 p + ... + nt p^t and k = k0 + k1 p + ... + kt p^t in base p. Then (n choose k) ≡ Π_{i=0}^t (n_i choose k_i) (mod p).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch: use (1+X)^n ≡ (1+X)^{n0} (1+X^p)^{n1} ... (1+X^{p^t})^{nt} (mod p) and compare coefficients. The text applies Lucas to deduce divisibility properties (e.g., p divides (p choose k) for 0<k<p) and to compute residues of binomial coefficients in many olympiad problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting binomial coefficients divisible by a prime via base-p digits
rubrics_metrics.description: Let p be prime and write n in base p as digits n_m ... n_1 n_0. Then the number of binomial coefficients (n choose k) that are multiples of p equals (n+1) − (n0+1)(n1+1)...(nm+1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a direct corollary of Lucas's theorem and is useful for combinatorial counting problems about parity or p-divisibility of Pascal's triangle rows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invariant-method guideline for combinatorial move problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Use invariants or monovariants (parity, product, sum, or other preserved quantities) to analyze reachability/impossibility in discrete move games. Examples in the text include checking products in rows/columns, linear combinations preserved by moves, or parity constraints to rule out or guarantee configurations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The section provides many model problems: e.g., computing row and column products on a ±1 board and deducing that certain global sums cannot be zero; or checking conserved linear combinations when stones/cards are moved. The recommended approach is to identify a simple invariant (or a monotone quantity) and use it to show impossibility or boundedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pompeiu/60°-rotation technique for equilateral-triangle problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply 60° rotations (Pompeiu theorem) about vertices of an equilateral triangle to relate distances and to construct associated Pompeiu triangles. The text uses 60° rotations to obtain angle relations (for instance deducing APB = 150° in an example), length relations, and inequalities like PA + PC ≥ PB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the rotation to map points and produce congruent or right triangles; derive equalities/inequalities among PA, PB, PC and use them for construction or locus problems. The text also shows how these rotations lead to the Pompeiu triangle and how to use it in constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area/barycentric and complex-coordinate methods for equilateral-locus problems
rubrics_metrics.description: For locus problems involving distances to vertices of an equilateral triangle, express signed areas k1 = S[PBC], k2 = S[PCA], k3 = S[PAB] and compute quantities like the Pompeiu-triangle area S[APP'] = k1 k2 + k1 k3 + k2 k3 and OP^2 in terms of k1,k2,k3 (leading to OP^2 = (1 − 3(k1k2 + k1k3 + k2k3)) OA^2). Alternatively, place A,B,C at 1, ω, ω^2 in the complex plane and show the Pompeiu-triangle area depends only on |x|, the distance of P from the center.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These computations reduce locus questions to conditions on |OP| (hence circles). The book gives both a barycentric/vector derivation and a complex-coordinate derivation; either yields that level sets of the Pompeiu-triangle area are circles centered at the centroid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for cyclic quadrilaterals used repeatedly
rubrics_metrics.description: A quadrilateral is cyclic if and only if a pair of opposite angles sum to 180°, or equivalently if it has two opposite right angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The geometry solutions repeatedly use these tests: show opposite angles add to 180° (often by angle chasing, rectangles, or arc measures) or exhibit two opposite right angles (e.g., via perpendicular projections) to conclude cyclicity. This is a core check used in many contest arguments on the page.
